metadata.title: Bloch Sphere — The Default That Buries the Inequality
metadata.purpose: viz-riff critique: Bloch sphere qubit visualization — Born rule encoding is honest; Robertson bound is trivially zero on first load because the default state sits on the xz-plane

beats.narration_text: Ciao. Liam, in for Bear. Someone asked Claude to write a Bloch sphere visualization — qubit state, Born rule bars, Robertson uncertainty panel. Today we are judging the visualization. The quantum mechanics gets a pass.

props.command: Hey Claude, write me a visualization for the Bloch sphere with qubit state controls and Robertson uncertainty.
output: ✓ Bloch sphere SVG — orthographic AZ=30° EL=25°
✓ θ/φ sliders → Born rule P(|0⟩) = cos²(θ/2)

beats.narration_text: Two columns. Left: a Bloch sphere in fixed orthographic projection, a red state-vector arrow, two dashed projection lines, two range sliders — theta and phi. Right: four panels. Born rule probabilities as live horizontal bar charts. The Bloch vector components to four decimal places. A Robertson uncertainty section with a ratio field. And a dark terminal called the Physics Console.

Drag theta from zero to one hundred eighty. At zero, the arrow points to the north pole — P of zero equals one, P of one equals zero. At ninety degrees, the bars split fifty-fifty. At one-eighty, south pole, probabilities flip. The Born rule is P of zero equals cosine-squared of theta over two. The slider IS that formula, updating in real time.

What it gets right. First: the Born rule formula is printed on screen beside the value it produces. The equation and the bar that instantiates it share the same frame — nothing requires looking up. Second: the Robertson inequality holds to machine precision everywhere on the sphere. At phi ninety, theta ninety — the plus-y state — the ratio column reads 1.0000, and a green checkmark confirms it. Equality is not claimed in prose; it is a reachable event the student can trigger. Third: the Physics Console lists five named checks with expected values at load. Students can read what the sim was tested against.

Two problems, both fixable. One: the default state is theta ninety, phi zero — the plus-x state, on the xz-plane. The Robertson panel opens showing zero greater than zero, labeled trivial. That is the least interesting Robertson scenario: the bound is vacuous because the commutator's expectation vanishes at phi zero and phi one-eighty. A student who never discovers the phi slider never sees a non-trivial inequality. The fix is one line: default phi to ninety degrees so the sim opens on the plus-y state and the ratio greets every visitor at 1.0000. Two: the Physics Console runs once at page load, then freezes. Drag the sliders; the console still shows the initial-state checks. It calls itself a physics checker but stops checking after second zero.

Let's recap with Claude. Born rule formula visible on screen alongside its bar — equation and value share one frame. Robertson equality demonstrable and reachable at phi ninety. Default phi-zero opens a trivial zero-greater-than-zero bound — the inequality is invisible on first load. Physics Console frozen at page-load, does not track live slider state. Useful for a lecture that has already introduced the Bloch sphere; not a self-paced first encounter.

artifactLines: Born rule formula on screen beside its bar — equation and value in one frame
Robertson equality demonstrable at θ=90°, φ=90° — ratio reaches 1.0000
Default φ=0° opens a trivial 0≥0 bound — inequality invisible on first load
Physics Console frozen at page-load — does not track live slider state

beats.narration_text: I built an interactive Bloch sphere simulation in single-file HTML using D3. It has theta and phi sliders, Born rule probability bars, a Bloch vector panel, and a Robertson uncertainty section computing Δσ_x · Δσ_z ≥ |⟨σ_y⟩|. Two fixes needed. One: change the default state from theta ninety phi zero to theta ninety phi ninety — the plus-y state — so the Robertson bound opens at ratio 1.0000 instead of the trivial zero-greater-than-zero case. Two: wire the physics-check function to both slider input events so the Physics Console updates on every move rather than running once at page load.
